groups.title: Angular's architecture and change detection model
groups.question: Your Angular view updates after an HTTP call without you telling it to, and a service you thought was shared has different data in two components. Explain how Angular tracks changes and provides services.

followUps.Zone.js and how Angular knows when to ru: How does Angular know it needs to update the view after an HTTP response?
followUps.Dependency injection: the hierarchical i: Why might two components get different instances of the same service?

evidence.text: Zone.js wraps async APIs like timers, events and HTTP so Angular knows when async work finishes.
Angular then runs change detection to compare bindings and update the view.
Work done outside Angular's zone does not trigger updates automatically.

notEnough: Only saying Angular uses change detection.

evidence.text: Angular resolves services by walking up a tree of injectors from the component to the root.
A service provided in root is a single shared instance.
A service provided in a component gets a new instance for that component and its children.

notEnough: Only saying Angular uses dependency injection.

groups.title: Component lifecycle hooks and template binding
groups.question: A component fetches data in its constructor and its inputs are undefined there, and a form field does not update the model. Explain the component lifecycle and the kinds of data binding.

followUps.ngOnInit vs constructor: when to initial: Why should data loading go in ngOnInit rather than the constructor?
followUps.Data binding: interpolation, property bi: What are the four kinds of data binding in Angular templates?

evidence.text: The constructor is for injecting dependencies.
ngOnInit runs after Angular has set the component's inputs.
ngOnDestroy is where subscriptions and timers are cleaned up.

notEnough: Only saying ngOnInit runs when the component starts.

evidence.text: Interpolation shows a value as text.
Property binding sets an element property from the component, and event binding calls a method when an event happens.
Two-way binding combines both, so the input and the model stay in sync.

groups.title: Building Angular components and using directives
groups.question: You are building a task list component that shows tasks only when loaded and repeats a row per task, using the Angular CLI. Explain the template features and the tooling.

followUps.Structural directives: *ngIf, *ngFor, an: What does the asterisk in *ngIf and *ngFor mean?
followUps.Angular CLI: generate, serve, build, and: What do the main Angular CLI commands do?

evidence.text: Structural directives add or remove elements from the page.
The asterisk is shorthand for wrapping the element in an ng-template.
ngIf renders conditionally and ngFor repeats an element for each item.

notEnough: Only saying they show and loop.

evidence.text: ng generate creates components, services and their test files.
ng serve runs a development server that reloads on changes.
ng build creates an optimized production build and ng test runs the tests.

groups.title: Services and the Angular router
groups.question: Several components need the same task data, and the app needs pages for the task list and task details. Explain how you would create services and set up routing.

followUps.Creating and injecting services with @In: How do you create a service shared across the whole app and use it in a component?
followUps.Angular Router: RouterModule, routes arr: How do routes, routerLink and router-outlet work together?

evidence.text: Marking a service injectable and provided in root makes one shared instance.
Components receive it through constructor injection or the inject function.
Creating it yourself with new skips dependency injection and loses sharing and testability.
A routes array maps paths to components.
router-outlet marks where the matched component appears.
routerLink navigates without a full page reload.

notEnough: Only saying Angular has a router.
